Fix \((G,T,e)\in\mathcal G_{n,k}\) and suppose \(d_e(G)<\infty\).  Multiplying the covariance identity on the left by \((I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) and on the right by \(I_n-\Lambda\) gives
\[
 \Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus every disturbance coordinate lies in \(K_G(\lambda_D)\), while the reverse inclusion follows from \(K_G\subseteq L\) and \(\lambda_D\subseteq L\).  Hence
\[
 L=K_G(\lambda_D).
\tag{2}
\]
Choose \(U\subseteq\lambda_D\setminus\{\lambda_e\}\) maximal algebraically independent over \(K_G\), put \(F=K_G(U)\), and enumerate the remaining coordinates as \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_q)\).  Since \(\lambda_e\) is algebraic over \(K_G\), maximality of \(U\) makes \(L/F\) finite.  It is separable because \(\operatorname{char}F=0\).  The minimal polynomial \(p\in K_G[t]\) of \(\lambda_e\) stays irreducible over the purely transcendental extension \(K_G(U)\): otherwise clearing denominators in a nontrivial factorization and specializing the algebraically independent variables \(U\) at a point of the infinite field \(K_G\), away from the finitely many denominator and leading-coefficient zeros, would factor \(p\) nontrivially over \(K_G\).  Therefore
\[
 [F(\lambda_e):F]=[K_G(\lambda_e):K_G]=d_e(G).
\tag{3}
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) and \(\mathrm{def:generic\mbox{-}fiber}\), after localizing at the nonzero elements of \(K_G[U]\), evaluation gives a surjection \(F[y]\to L\) whose kernel is generated by the missing-bidirected residuals.  For the minimal polynomial \(g_a\in F[t]\) of \(y_a\), there are \(c_{a,ij}\in F[y]\) such that
\[
 g_a(y_a)=\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y)F_{ij}(y).
\tag{4}
\]
Differentiating in \(\Omega_{L/F}\), then using \(F_{ij}(y)=0\), yields
\[
 g_a'(y_a),dy_a
 =\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y),dF_{ij}.
\tag{5}
\]
Separability gives \(g_a'(y_a)\ne0\).  Hence the evaluated residual gradients span all \(dy_a\), and the residual Jacobian with respect to \(y\) has rank \(q\).  Select residuals \(f_1,\ldots,f_q\) with nonzero Jacobian determinant \(\Delta\in L\).

There are exactly \(d_e(G)\) distinct \(F\)-embeddings of \(F(\lambda_e)\) into \(\overline F\), by (3).  Each extends to an \(F\)-embedding of the finite separable extension \(L/F\), by adjoining the remaining algebraic generators and choosing a root of each transported minimal polynomial.  Such an embedding is a common zero of \(f_1,\ldots,f_q\), and it sends \(\Delta\) to a nonzero element.  It is therefore a nonsingular isolated zero.  Embeddings with distinct restrictions to \(F(\lambda_e)\) have distinct \(\lambda_e\)-coordinates.

Partition \(y\) into nonempty blocks indexed by child vertices, and let \(r_v\) be the size of the block indexed by \(v\).  Then
\[
 1\le r_v\le\operatorname{indeg}_D(v).
\tag{6}
\]
The displayed formula for \(F_{ij}\) is affine-linear in each of its two child blocks.  Thus a selected residual meeting one remaining block is unary, and a residual meeting two is bilinear of multidegree at most one in each block.  Decompose the equation--block incidence graph into connected components.  A nonzero monomial in \(\Delta\) supplies a row--column matching, so every component contains equally many equations and variables.

In the component containing \(\lambda_e\), let \(b\) be the number of blocks, \(u\) the number of unary equations, and \(m_H\) the number of binary equations.  If \(b>1\), the binary equations form a connected simple graph \(H\): connectivity follows from the component definition, and simplicity follows because an unordered pair of child vertices supplies only one residual.  For \(b=1\), let \(H\) be the one-vertex graph.  Squareness gives
\[
 \sum_{v\in V(H)}r_v=u+m_H.
\tag{7}
\]
The isolated-zero bound \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) bounds the number of isolated zeros of this component by the coefficient of \(\prod_vX_v^{r_v}\) in
\[
 \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{u}X_{v(\ell)}\right)
 \left(\prod_{\{v,w\}\in E(H)}(X_v+X_w)\right).
\tag{8}
\]
After subtracting the fixed unary exponents, this is \(c_H(s)\) for one prescribed nonnegative indegree vector \(s\); a negative coordinate would make the coefficient zero, contrary to the already exhibited isolated solutions.  Each conjugate of \(\lambda_e\) supplies a distinct zero in this component, so
\[
 d_e(G)\le c_H(s).
\tag{9}
\]

The root of the supplied arborescence has no incoming directed edge: an arrow into it together with the tree path from the root to that arrow's tail would create a directed cycle, contrary to \(\mathrm{ass:acyclic}\).  Hence it has no nonempty child block, and
\[
 b\le n-1.
\tag{10}
\]
For \(b>1\), put \(g_H=m_H-b+1\).  Equations (6)--(7), nonnegativity of \(u\), and \(\mathrm{ass:arborescence}\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_H
 &=\sum_{v\in V(H)}r_v-u-b+1\\
 &\le\sum_{v\in V(H)}\bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &\le\sum_{v\ne\operatorname{root}(T)}
       \bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &=|D|-n+2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The omitted summands are nonnegative because every nonroot vertex has its incoming tree arrow.  If \(b=1\), set \(g_H=0\); then the same bound follows from \(|D|\ge|T|=n-1\).  Thus (9)--(11) and \(\mathrm{def:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) imply
\[
 d_e(G)\le\vartheta_{n-1,\,|D|-n+2}.
\tag{12}
\]
Since \(T\subseteq D\), \(|T|=n-1\), and \(\mathrm{ass:excess\mbox{-}budget}\) holds,
\[
 |D|-n+2=|D\setminus T|+1\le k+1.
\tag{13}
\]
Monotonicity and the bounds proved in \(\mathrm{lem:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) now give
\[
 d_e(G)\le\vartheta_{n-1,\,|D|-n+2}
 \le\vartheta_{n-1,k+1}
 \le\min\{2^{k+1},\tau_{n-1}\},
\tag{14}
\]
and, before applying (13),
\[
 d_e(G)\le\min\{2^{|D|-n+2},\tau_{n-1}\}.
\tag{15}
\]
Maximizing (14) over the finite-degree members of \(\mathcal G_{n,k}\) proves \(D_k(n)\le\vartheta_{n-1,k+1}\).  The argument only isolated the queried component and therefore remains valid when other generic-fiber components are positive dimensional.

For \(n=6\), the exact values in \(\mathrm{lem:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) are \(\vartheta_{5,3}=6\), \(\vartheta_{5,4}=8\), \(\vartheta_{5,5}=12\), and \(\vartheta_{5,g}=24\) for \(g\ge6\).  Substitution of \(g=k+1\) proves
\[
 D_2(6)\le6,\qquad D_3(6)\le8,\qquad D_4(6)\le12,
 \qquad D_k(6)\le24\quad(k\ge5),
\]
for every admissible \(k\).

Put \(d=k+1\) and \(N=2d+2=2k+4\).  In the \(N\)-vertex graph of \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), the arrows are
\[
 0\to P_i,\qquad 0\to Q_i,\qquad P_i\to h
 \quad(1\le i\le d).
\]
The supplied set consists of the first \(2d\) arrows and \(P_1\to h\).  Therefore
\[
 |T|=2d+1=N-1,qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\le i\le d\},qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.
\tag{16}
\]
Every nonroot vertex has one incoming tree arrow, every vertex is reached from \(0\), and the order \(0,(P_i,Q_i)_{i=1}^d,h\) is topological.  Thus \((G^{\star}_{k,N},T,e^{\star})\in\mathcal G_{N,k}\).

Choose positive rational \(h_i\) and rational \(b_i\) satisfying \(b_i^2>4h_i\), and put \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  Choose a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\), sufficiently close to \(H_0\), with the same diagonal; below we impose one further generic restriction on its off-diagonal entries.  In the order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), set
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0&0&1\\
  0&H&H&0\\
  0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
  1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{17}
\]
Choose rational \(C_0\) with \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  The Schur complement of \(H\) proves that the \((P,Q)\)-principal block is positive definite.  Adding the independent \(0\)-coordinate preserves this property, and choosing rational \(M\) above the final Schur-complement threshold gives
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}\succ0.
\tag{18}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\quad c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\quad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\quad z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},
 \quad x=-Hz.
\]
The missing pairs are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\).  Direct substitution of (17) in the definition of \(F_{ij}\) gives
\[
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i,qquad
 0=h_i+a_ic_i.
\tag{19}
\]
Since \(H\) is invertible, these equations are equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,qquad c_i=x_i+b_i,qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0\quad(1\le i\le d),qquad
 z=-H^{-1}x.
\tag{20}
\]
Every quadratic in (20) has positive discriminant, so there are exactly \(2^d\) real solutions.  Under the invertible change \(z\mapsto x=-Hz\), the residual Jacobian in \((a,c,z)\) is nonsingular exactly when
\[
 \det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.
\tag{21}
\]
Indeed, for fixed \(i\) the three equations in \((a_i,c_i,x_i)\) have determinant, up to sign, \(a_i+c_i=2x_i+b_i\), and at a solution
\[
 (2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0.
\]
Thus all \(2^d\) points are reduced.  Defining
\[
 \Omega=(I_N-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{\star}(I_N-\Lambda)
\tag{22}
\]
makes precisely the missing-pair entries vanish by (19).  The topological order makes \(I_N-\Lambda\) unit triangular, so (18) and congruence imply \(\Omega\succ0\).  Hence every solution is a real supported positive-definite source lift.

We next choose \(H\) so that \(z_1=\lambda_{e^{\star}}\) separates the solutions.  At \(H=H_0\), branches with different first coordinate \(x_1\) already have different \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If branch vectors \(x\ne x'\) have the same first coordinate, choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and set \(H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1})\).  Differentiating the inverse gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\{z_1(x)-z_1(x')\}\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.
\tag{23}
\]
Thus equality of the two first coordinates after applying \(-H^{-1}\) is a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  There are finitely many branch pairs.  Their proper algebraic sets cannot cover a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\), and rational matrices are dense, so a rational positive-definite \(H\) can be chosen outside their union.  Its \(2^d\) values of \(z_1\) are distinct.

There are \(3d\) directed coordinates and \(3d\) missing residuals.  Since all other pairs are bidirected,
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left(\binom N2-3d\right)+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2=:M_0.
\tag{24}
\]
Perturb the independent covariance coordinates as \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\), where the \(M_0\) entries of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent.  At any reduced solution \(v_0=(a,c,z)\), seek a formal solution \(v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\ge1}v_r(\xi)\), with \(v_r\) homogeneous of degree \(r\).  At degree \(r\), the residual equations read
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}).
\tag{25}
\]
The Jacobian is invertible by (21), so (25) uniquely determines every \(v_r\).  Each displayed point therefore has a formal section over the full covariance formal neighborhood.

If \(f\in P_G\), substitution of any section gives \(f(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi)=0\) in \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\).  Translation by \(\Sigma^{\star}\) is injective on the covariance polynomial ring and the coordinates of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent, so \(f=0\).  Hence
\[
 P_G=(0),\qquad K_G=\mathbb C(\sigma_{ij}:i\le j).
\tag{26}
\]
Equation (24) now shows that \(L\) and \(K_G\) have equal transcendence degree; hence the finitely generated extension \(L/K_G\) is finite.

Partition the directed variables into singleton blocks \(A_i=(a_i)\), singleton blocks \(C_i=(c_i)\), and the size-\(d\) block \(Z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\).  The residual block degrees are bounded by \(A_i+C_i\), \(A_i+Z\), and \(C_i+Z\), respectively.  The multihomogeneous isolated-zero bound gives
\[
 [L:K_G]\le
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^dA_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.
\tag{27}
\]
For each \(i\), precisely two selections contribute \(A_iC_iZ\), proving the coefficient equality.

Conversely, every formal section defines a homomorphism from the integral incidence ring to \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\) restricting to the same injective covariance translation.  Its image has transcendence degree at least \(M_0\), equal by (24) to the dimension of the incidence domain, so its prime kernel has height zero and is zero.  Passing to fraction fields produces \(2^d\) distinct \(K_G\)-embeddings of \(L\) into \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]]\); they send \(z_1\) to series with distinct constant terms.  Consequently
\[
 2^d\le[K_G(z_1):K_G]\le[L:K_G]\le2^d.
\tag{28}
\]
Thus \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,N})=2^{k+1}\), and the original coefficient \(e^{\star}\) separates all conjugate branches.  Characteristic zero makes the minimal polynomial separable.  Clearing its coefficient denominators and excluding their zeros and its nonzero discriminant gives a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set on which the roots remain distinct; \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) identifies them with the finite queried-coordinate projection.

For \(n>N\), append a fully bidirected child \(w\) of \(0\), and place \(0\to w\) in \(T\).  No missing residual involves \(w\).  Conditional on the old source coordinates and \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\), covariance congruence is an invertible triangular polynomial change between the new allowed disturbance coordinates and the new covariance row \(s_w\).  Hence
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,s_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(s_w),
\tag{29}
\]
with \(x_w\) and the entries of \(s_w\) algebraically independent over \(L_0\).  Irreducibility is preserved by the purely transcendental extension \(K_0(s_w)/K_0\), so
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.
\tag{30}
\]
Iteration proves the degree assertion for every \(n\ge2k+4\), while membership is preserved because each new arrow is a tree arrow.  Finally \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) gives \(D_k(n)\le2^{k+1}\), whereas (28)--(30) give the reverse inequality.  Therefore
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\ge2k+4),
\]
with the claimed nonempty Zariski-open separation set.

Put \(r=|D\setminus T|\).  This integer is read from the input, so \(r=0\) and \(r>0\) are deterministic, mutually exclusive, and exhaustive.

If \(r=0\), \(\mathrm{lem:tree\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}algorithm\mbox{-}transfer}\) identifies \(\mathcal G_{n,0}\) exactly with the published rooted-tree mixed-graph class, including arbitrary bidirected support.  Run that procedure with tolerance \(\delta\).  In the finite case it proves \(d_e(G)\in\{1,2\}\) and returns all \(d_e(G)\) generic values as \(\operatorname{FASTP}\) expressions \((\rho_i)\), giving the first output row in \(\mathrm{def:certificate\mbox{-}algorithm}\).  In the infinite case it returns \((\operatorname{tree},\infty)\), giving the second row.  The transfer lemma supplies error probability at most \(\delta\).

Assume henceforth that \(r>0\), and enumerate the source coordinates as
\[
 u=(\lambda_D,\omega_B,\omega_{\mathrm{diag}})=(u_1,\ldots,u_N),
 \qquad N=|D|+|B|+n.
\]
Then \(L=\mathbb C(u_1,\ldots,u_N)\).  By \(\mathrm{ass:acyclic}\), a topological order makes \(\Lambda\) strictly triangular and \(\Lambda^n=0\), whence
\[
 (I_n-\Lambda)^{-1}=I_n+\Lambda+\cdots+\Lambda^{n-1}.
\tag{31}
\]
Thus each covariance coordinate
\[
 s_{ij}(u)=\phi_G(\sigma_{ij})
 =[(I_n-\Lambda)^{-\mathsf T}\Omega(I_n-\Lambda)^{-1}]_{ij}
\]
is a polynomial of degree at most \(2n-1\) and has an arithmetic circuit of size polynomial in \(n\).  Let \(J_0=\partial s/\partial u\), and let \(J_1\) be obtained by adjoining the row \(\partial\lambda_e/\partial u\).  Entries of \(J_0\) have degree at most \(2n-2\), and the added row has degree zero.

We prove the required rank criterion.  For \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in L\), put \(F_0=\mathbb C(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\) and choose a maximal algebraically independent subfamily \(b_1,\ldots,b_q\).  Extend it by \(c_1,\ldots,c_\ell\) to a transcendence basis of \(L/\mathbb C\).  The remaining extension is finite separable because the characteristic is zero.  The derivation of the rational-function field that maps one \(b_j\) to \(1\) and all other \(b\)'s and \(c\)'s to zero extends through a finite separable extension: if \(v\) has minimal polynomial \(g\), differentiation of \(g(v)=0\) uniquely forces
\[
 g'(v),dv=-\sum_hv^h,dg_h,
\]
and \(g'(v)\ne0\).  Applying these derivations proves that \(db_1,\ldots,db_q\) are linearly independent over \(L\).  Conversely, differentiating the separable minimal polynomial of each \(a_i\) expresses \(da_i\) in their span.  Therefore
\[
 \dim_L\operatorname{span}_L\{da_1,\ldots,da_m\}
 =\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(a_1,\ldots,a_m).
\tag{32}
\]
Applying (32) to the covariance coordinates and then to those coordinates together with \(\lambda_e\) gives
\[
 \operatorname{rank}_LJ_0=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}K_G,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}_LJ_1=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}K_G(\lambda_e).
\tag{33}
\]
Adjoining one element preserves transcendence degree exactly when it is algebraic and otherwise raises it by one.  Hence equal ranks are equivalent to \(d_e(G)<\infty\), while a rank increase by one is equivalent to \(d_e(G)=\infty\).

Acyclicity and the definition of bidirected support imply
\[
 N=|D|+|B|+n\le n^2.
\]
There are at most \(n(n+1)/2+1\le n^2+1\) rows.  A determinant witnessing either generic rank therefore has total degree at most
\[
 (n^2+1)(2n-2)\le2n^3
\]
for \(n\ge2\), using \(\mathrm{ass:size}\).  Sample each source coordinate independently and uniformly from a finite rational set \(S\) with \(|S|\ge\lceil4n^3/\delta\rceil\).  Evaluation cannot increase rank.  If the evaluated rank drops, a fixed nonzero maximal minor vanishes.  By \(\mathrm{lem:schwartz\mbox{-}zippel\mbox{-}bound}\), this has probability at most \(\delta/2\) for each Jacobian.  A union bound proves that both evaluated ranks are generic with probability at least \(1-\delta\).  Exact evaluation points, pivots, evaluated minors, and identity-test records form \(\mathcal J_{G,e}\).

On this error-free event, if the augmented rank is larger, then \(\lambda_e\) is transcendental over \(K_G\).  The map
\[
 K_G[t]\longrightarrow A_K,qquad t\longmapsto\lambda_e,
\]
is injective.  By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), \(A_K\) is integral with fraction field \(L\), so this map induces a dominant morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}(A_K)\to\mathbb A^1_{K_G}\).  Moreover \(\dim A_K=\operatorname{trdeg}_{K_G}L\ge1\).  The source-parametric incidence equations and augmented-rank transcript consequently give the dominance certificate \(\mathcal N_{G,e}\), proving the fourth output row.

If the ranks agree, then \(d_e(G)<\infty\).  By \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) and \(\mathrm{lem:tournament\mbox{-}score\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}ceiling}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 d_e(G)
 &\le\min\{2^{|D|-n+2},\tau_{n-1}\}\\
 &\le\min\{2^{|D|-n+2},2^{\binom{n-2}{2}}\}
 =2^{\min\{|D|-n+2,\binom{n-2}{2}\}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{34}
\]
Since \(|T|=n-1\), one has \(|D|-n+2=r+1\le k+1\), and therefore
\[
 d_e(G)\le2^{\min\{|D|-n+2,\binom{n-2}{2}\}}
 \le2^{\min\{k+1,\binom{n-2}{2}\}}.
\tag{35}
\]
This proves the third output row.  The rank test and bound do not calculate the exact degree, \(p_e\), \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\), or \(h_{G,e}\), exactly as the theorem states.

The tree branch has randomized polynomial cost by the transfer lemma.  On the positive-excess branch, (31), the covariance products, circuit differentiation, exact specialization, and Gaussian elimination on matrices of dimensions at most \((n^2+1)\times n^2\) all have polynomial arithmetic cost.  A sampled coordinate needs \(O(\log n+\log(1/\delta))\) bits; separate bit cost is excluded by \(\mathsf{ArithmeticModel}\).  Thus one universal \(C>0\) bounds construction time and transcript length on either branch by
\[
 n^{C(k+1)}\operatorname{poly}(\log(1/\delta)),
\]
since \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge0\).  Only one branch is executed, and the preceding error allocation bounds total symbolic error by \(\delta\).  All four outputs and their mutual exclusivity follow.

Condition on the successful event in \(\mathrm{thm:conditional\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\), whose probability is at least \(1-\delta\).  Every circuit retained in \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\) has nonzero pullback under the covariance parametrization.  Its class in the integral domain \(R_G\cong\operatorname{im}\phi_G\) is therefore nonzero.  Their finite product is nonzero, so \(h_{G,e}\) is not the zero polynomial on the model image and
\[
 \mathcal E_{G,e}=V(h_{G,e})
\tag{43}
\]
is proper there.

The relation \(p_e(\lambda_e)=0\) holds in \(A_K\).  Clearing only covariance denominators gives \(a\in S_G\) and incidence polynomials \(c_{ij}\) such that
\[
 a(\Sigma)p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)
 =\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}
 c_{ij}(\Sigma,\Lambda)F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma).
\tag{44}
\]
The factor \(a\) is among the covariance-localization circuits.  If \(h_{G,e}(\Sigma)\ne0\), every solution of all specialized residuals therefore satisfies \(p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)=0\).  By the definition of \(\mathcal Z_e\),
\[
 \mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma)
 \subseteq\{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}.
\tag{45}
\]

For the converse, set \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  For every \(K_G\)-embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the algebra \(L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}\) is nonzero.  The coordinate-preserving slices in the conditional construction were chosen from a common open set meeting each conjugate component.  Their rational univariate representations consequently contain every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\).  By \(\mathrm{lem:generic\mbox{-}rur\mbox{-}specialization}\), these representations specialize with finite points and multiplicities preserved away from loci where dimension, a denominator, a leading coefficient, a point at infinity, or separation degenerates.  Every such locus contributes a factor to \(h_{G,e}\).  The incidence-lifting identities verify by substitution that each specialized univariate point satisfies every original residual.  Hence every root of the specialized polynomial lifts to the original incidence scheme, and
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
 \subseteq\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{46}
\]
The slice is used only to construct the certificate; the lifting identities return to \(I_G\), so no zero-dimensionality of the unsliced \(\Lambda\)-fiber is required.

Equations (45)--(46) prove the asserted equality.  Pole and incidence-lifting factors retain components on which an intermediate expression has a pole or is identically zero-over-zero.  Projective-leading-form and specialized-leading-coefficient factors prevent exchange with infinity and degree drop.  Finally, characteristic zero makes \(p_e\) separable over \(K_G\); outside the squarefreeness resultant factor, its specialization remains squarefree.  Thus all displayed roots are distinct.

Write \(s=(s_{ij}:i\le j)\) for real symmetric covariance variables, \(z\) for the queried value, and \(\ell=(\ell_f:f\in D)\) for real directed-coefficient variables.  Define
\[
 \Phi_G(s,z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists\ell\in\mathbb R^D\left[
   \ell_e=z\ \wedge\
   \bigwedge_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}F_{ij}(\ell,s)=0
 \right].
\tag{47}
\]
All polynomials in (47) have rational coefficients: \(D\) and \(B\) only select variables and equations, while the residual coefficients are \(0,1,-1\).  By \(\mathrm{def:real\mbox{-}retained\mbox{-}set}\),
\[
 \Phi_G(\Sigma,z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{48}
\]
Apply \(\mathrm{lem:effective\mbox{-}real\mbox{-}quantifier\mbox{-}elimination}\) with \(\ell\) quantified and \((s,z)\) free.  It effectively produces a finite Boolean combination
\[
 \Psi_G(s,z)=\bigvee_a\bigwedge_b
 \bigl(\operatorname{sign}g_{ab}(s,z)=\epsilon_{ab}\bigr),
 \qquad g_{ab}\in\mathbb Q[s,z],\quad
 \epsilon_{ab}\in\{-1,0,1\},
\tag{49}
\]
equivalent to \(\Phi_G\) over the real closed field \(\mathbb R\).  Equations (48)--(49) give the required computable if-and-only-if condition.  Since (47) uses the original residuals and performs no division, it includes positive-dimensional fibers and components in denominator-zero loci.

Under the valid-chart and successful-output antecedents, if \(\Sigma\succ0\) is real, in the model image, and outside \(\mathcal E_{G,e}\), then \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\) gives
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}=\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{50}
\]
The nonzero squarefreeness factor makes each root simple.  Formula (49) therefore decides, root by root, precisely whether a real root has a complete real supported extension.  Nothing in this step infers real uniqueness from complex degree or from a local rank.

Now suppose the entries of \(\Sigma\) are real algebraic with exact univariate representations and isolating data.  Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) is exactly evaluable because all certified denominators are nonzero.  Clear a known nonzero common denominator.  Applied to the resulting univariate equation, \(\mathrm{lem:real\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}sampling}\) returns a point on every semialgebraically connected component of its real zero set.  Squarefreeness makes those components the individual roots; exact sign determination orders them and gives disjoint isolating intervals.

For such a root \(z\), exact sign determination evaluates (49).  Equivalently, define
\[
 Q_{\Sigma,z}(\ell)
 =(\ell_e-z)^2+
 \sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}F_{ij}(\ell,\Sigma)^2.
\tag{51}
\]
Over an ordered field a sum of squares vanishes exactly when every summand does, and hence
\[
 Z_{\mathbb R}(Q_{\Sigma,z})\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Phi_G(\Sigma,z)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{52}
\]
In the accepting case, real algebraic sampling applied to (51), over the ordered algebraic coefficient domain generated by \(\Sigma,z\), returns a real univariate representation of a full lift \(\ell\).  In the rejecting case, the evaluated sign vector in (49) certifies failure.  A finite tower of real algebraic coefficients has a primitive-element encoding: only finitely many rational linear combinations fail to separate the conjugate tuples, and an isolating interval selects the intended real embedding.  Thus the root representation, its isolating interval, the exact sign data, and, when accepted, the sample-point representation form a finite \(\mathsf{LiftCert}\) accepting exactly the elements of \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).

Finally, let \(\Lambda\in\mathbb R^D\) be an accepted lift and put \(R=I_n-\Lambda\).  Acyclicity makes \(R\) unit triangular in a topological order and hence invertible.  Define
\[
 \Omega=R^{\mathsf T}\Sigma R.
\tag{53}
\]
For nonzero real \(x\), \(Rx\ne0\), so
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}\Omega x=(Rx)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(Rx)>0.
\]
Thus \(\Omega\succ0\).  Entrywise expansion of (53) is \(\Omega_{ij}=F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma)\).  The accepting equations make it zero whenever \(i\leftrightarrow j\notin B\), exactly the restriction in \(\mathrm{ass:noise\mbox{-}support}\).  Conversely, every real supported SEM lift satisfies these residual equations.  Rearranging (53) recovers \(\Sigma=R^{-\mathsf T}\Omega R^{-1}\), proving that the certificate retains all and only the real supported extensions and that positive definiteness follows by congruence.

Work under the valid-chart and successful-output antecedents.  By \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\), \(h_{G,e}\) is nonzero in the covariance-model coordinate ring.  Identify the free real entries of supported \((\Lambda,\Omega)\) with \(\mathbb R^N\), where \(N=|D|+|B|+n\).  The supported positive-definite source set
\[
 \mathcal S_+=\{(\Lambda,\Omega)\in\mathbb R^N:\Omega\succ0\}
\tag{54}
\]
is nonempty, since it contains \((0,I_n)\), and Euclidean open, since strict positive definiteness is stable under small perturbations.  It is Zariski dense in the corresponding complex source space: it contains a real open box around \((0,I_n)\), and a complex polynomial vanishing on that box is zero by treating it successively as a univariate polynomial in each coordinate.

For the fixed acyclic graph define
\[
 \Phi_G(\Lambda,\Omega)
 =(I_n-\Lambda)^{-\mathsf T}\Omega(I_n-\Lambda)^{-1}.
\tag{55}
\]
In a topological order \(\Lambda^n=0\), so the inverse is the finite polynomial \(I_n+\Lambda+\cdots+\Lambda^{n-1}\), and \(\Phi_G\) is polynomial.  Nonzeroness of \(h_{G,e}\) in \(R_G\) says that \(h_{G,e}\circ\Phi_G\) is a nonzero source polynomial.  Zariski density of (54) supplies \((\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\in\mathcal S_+\) such that
\[
 h_{G,e}(\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0))\ne0.
\]
With \(\Sigma_0=\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\), this is
\[
 \Sigma_0\in\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}.
\tag{56}
\]

The model image is semialgebraic: it is the projection of the set defined by the polynomial covariance identities, the linear missing-support equations, and the strict principal-minor inequalities for \(\Omega\succ0\); effective real quantifier elimination removes the source variables.  The exceptional complement and all real-lifting sign conditions are semialgebraic.  Away from the leading-coefficient and squarefreeness factors, the degree of \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) is fixed and all its roots are simple.  The property that \(z\) is the \(j\)-th ordered real root is an ordered-field formula.  Quantifier elimination makes its graph semialgebraic, and intersecting with the lifting formula and projecting makes each ordered root's extendability locus semialgebraic.

Apply \(\mathrm{lem:semialgebraic\mbox{-}stratification}\) to the finite common refinement by the model image, exceptional complement, real-root counts, and extendability loci, and then take connected components.  The component containing \(\Sigma_0\) is a connected smooth semialgebraic cell
\[
 \mathcal C_{G,e}\subseteq\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}
\tag{57}
\]
on which the number of simple real roots and every ordered root's extension label are constant.  This is a cell allowed by \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}cell}\).

Choose a smooth coordinate chart \(u:U\to u(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^s\) around \(\Sigma_0\).  If \(s>0\), choose \(\rho>0\) with \(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)\subset u(U)\), and put
\[
 \mathcal K_G=u^{-1}(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)).
\tag{58}
\]
If \(s=0\), put \(\mathcal K_G=\{\Sigma_0\}\).  In either case this set is nonempty, compact, and has nonempty relative interior in \(\mathcal C_{G,e}\), as required by \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}class}\).

For every \(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G\), membership in \(\mathcal M_G\) supplies real supported \(\Lambda\) and \(\Omega\succ0\) satisfying (55).  Rearrangement gives \(\Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda)\), whose missing-pair entries are exactly \(F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma)=0\).  Thus the real value \(\lambda_e\) has a complete supported extension and belongs to \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).  Hence \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\) throughout \(\mathcal K_G\).

Put \(d=d_e(G)\).  On the successful output,
\[
 p_e(\Sigma,t)=t^d+\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}c_a(\Sigma)t^a.
\tag{59}
\]
Each \(c_a\) is a rational covariance circuit.  Since \(\mathcal K_G\subset\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}\), every denominator, specialized-leading-coefficient, and squarefreeness factor is continuous and nonzero there.  Compactness gives a positive minimum for each denominator and a finite maximum for each numerator.  Thus some \(M<\infty\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{0\le a<d}|c_a(\Sigma)|\le M
 \quad(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G).
\tag{60}
\]
If \(z\) is a root and \(|z|>1+M\), then
\[
 |z|^d\le M\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}|z|^a
 =M\frac{|z|^d-1}{|z|-1}<|z|^d,
\]
a contradiction.  Hence all roots lie in \(|z|\le1+M\).  The root-incidence set
\[
 \mathcal Z_{\mathrm{root}}
 =\{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathcal K_G\times\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
\tag{61}
\]
is closed in a compact set and therefore compact.

The nonzero squarefreeness certificate says that \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) and \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) have no common root.  Hence \(\partial_tp_e\ne0\) on (61), and continuity gives
\[
 \eta=\min_{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{root}}}
 |\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,z)|>0.
\tag{62}
\]
If no uniform separation existed, there would be \(\Sigma_\nu\in\mathcal K_G\) and distinct roots \(z_\nu,w_\nu\) with \(|z_\nu-w_\nu|\to0\).  A convergent subsequence would satisfy \(\Sigma_\nu\to\Sigma_*\) and \(z_\nu,w_\nu\to z_*\).  The divided difference
\[
 \frac{p_e(\Sigma,z)-p_e(\Sigma,w)}{z-w}
\]
extends polynomially to \(z=w\), with value \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,z)\).  It vanishes along the sequence, so the limit gives both \(p_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0\) and \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0\), contradicting (62).  Thus some \(\gamma>0\) uniformly separates all distinct complex roots.  Every retained real value is one of those roots by exceptional-set validity and real-root lifting, so the same \(\gamma\) separates retained roots.

Let \(q=n(n+1)/2\), fix an ordering \(\operatorname{vech}\) of symmetric entries, and set
\[
 W_r=\operatorname{vech}\!\left(X^{(r)}X^{(r)\mathsf T}-\Sigma\right).
\]
Then
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 =m^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^mW_r.
\tag{63}
\]
Under \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}gaussian}\), the summands are independent and centered.  Differentiation of the Gaussian moment-generating function gives
\[
 \mathbb E(X_iX_jX_kX_l)
 =\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{kl}+\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}
  +\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk},
\]
and therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(W_{r,ij},W_{r,kl})
 =\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}+\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk}
 =(V_\Sigma)_{ij,kl}.
\tag{64}
\]
Compactness of \(\mathcal K_G\) uniformly bounds every fixed Gaussian moment, including \(\mathbb E_\Sigma\|W_r\|^3\).  For fixed \(u\in\mathbb R^q\), Taylor's formula for the characteristic function yields, uniformly in \(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\Sigma\exp\!\left(
 \frac{iu^{\mathsf T}W_r}{\sqrt m}\right)
 =1-\frac{u^{\mathsf T}V_\Sigma u}{2m}+O(m^{-3/2}).
\tag{65}
\]
Taking the \(m\)-th power proves the covariance central limit law.  Uniformity follows by the subsequence principle: every sequence in the compact set has a convergent subsequence, (65) identifies every weak subsequential limit, and uniformly bounded second moments give tightness.  Hence
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,V_\Sigma)
\tag{66}
\]
uniformly over \(\mathcal K_G\), while Chebyshev's inequality gives
\[
 \|S_m-\Sigma\|=O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\tag{67}
\]
uniformly.

Write \(\widehat\Sigma_m=\pi_G(S_m)\) on the projection tube.  Since \(\pi_G(\Sigma)=\Sigma\) on the smooth stratum, smoothness and compactness give
\[
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 =D\pi_G(\Sigma)\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
  +O_{\mathbb P}(\|S_m-\Sigma\|^2)
\tag{68}
\]
uniformly.  Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) is smooth near \(\mathcal K_G\), since its denominator has a positive uniform margin.  The derived separation lemma supplies a common separation margin and a positive lower bound for \(|\partial_tp_e|\).  The equation \(p_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))=0\) therefore gives one unique smooth branch through each retained root, with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on a finite cover, and
\[
 Dr_j(\Sigma)[H]
 =-\frac{D_\Sigma p_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))[H]}
         {\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))}.
\tag{69}
\]
Increasing order, separation, and constancy of extension labels on the connected regular cell give the common labeling \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_J)\).  Equations (66)--(69), Taylor's formula, and Slutsky's argument yield
\[
 \sqrt m\{r(\pi_G(S_m))-r(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N\!\left(0,
 Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}
 \right)
\tag{70}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\).

All certificate factors are continuous and nonzero on \(\mathcal K_G\), and extension labels are locally constant on the selected cell.  Compactness supplies a relative neighborhood \(U\) on which the projection is defined, every certificate remains valid, and the same \(J\) branches are retained.  With \(\gamma\) from the separation lemma, define
\[
 \mathcal H_m=\left\{
 \begin{array}{l}
 S_m\text{ lies in the projection tube},\quad
 \widehat\Sigma_m\in U,\\[2pt]
 \displaystyle\max_{1\le j\le J}
 |r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|<\gamma/3
 \end{array}\right\}.
\tag{71}
\]
Uniform consistency in (67)--(68), uniform continuity of the roots, and the positive certificate margins imply
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m)\longrightarrow1.
\tag{72}
\]
On \(\mathcal H_m\), real-root lifting and \(\mathrm{def:finite\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}estimator}\) give
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}
 =\{r_1(\widehat\Sigma_m),\ldots,r_J(\widehat\Sigma_m)\}.
\tag{73}
\]
The margin in (71) makes (73) a bijective matching to \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).  The regular-cell lemma gives \(J\ge1\), so the estimated set is nonempty.  Moreover,
\[
 d_H(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m},\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma))
 \le\max_j|r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|
 =O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\tag{74}
\]
uniformly.  Although the stipulated distance may be infinite on \(\mathcal H_m^c\), (72) makes that event uniformly negligible, which is precisely the uniform \(O_{\mathbb P}\) assertion.  Also
\[
 \sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\varnothing)
 \le\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m^c)
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{75}
\]

For simultaneous neighborhoods, let \(s=\dim\mathcal C_{G,e}\) and
\[
 W_\pi(\Sigma)=D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
For any nonzero symmetric direction \(H\), (64) implies
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\Sigma(X^{\mathsf T}HX)
 =2\operatorname{tr}\!\left((\Sigma^{1/2}H\Sigma^{1/2})^2\right)>0.
\tag{76}
\]
Thus \(V_\Sigma\) is positive definite on symmetric-coordinate directions.  The nearest-point projection fixes the stratum, so its derivative is the identity on the tangent space and has that \(s\)-dimensional space as its image.  Hence \(W_\pi\) has constant rank \(s\).  Compactness bounds its smallest positive eigenvalue away from zero, making its Moore--Penrose inverse continuous.  With the continuous plug-in matrix \(\widehat W_{\pi,m}\), (66)--(68) and continuous mapping give
\[
 m\,\operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}
 \widehat W_{\pi,m}^{+}
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow\chi_s^2
\tag{77}
\]
uniformly.  If \(Z\sim N(0,W_\pi)\), diagonalization of \(W_\pi\) shows directly that \(Z^{\mathsf T}W_\pi^+Z\) is a sum of \(s\) independent squared standard normals.

Let \(E_m\) be the corresponding confidence ellipsoid centered at \(\widehat\Sigma_m\), intersected with the regular projected neighborhood, and using the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\chi_s^2\).  Equation (77) gives
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\Sigma\in E_m)\ge1-\alpha.
\tag{78}
\]
For \(s=0\), use the degenerate ellipsoid at the locally constant projected point, whose limiting coverage is one.  Set \(\mathcal A_{m,j}=r_j(E_m)\), as in \(\mathrm{def:branch\mbox{-}neighborhoods}\).  Whenever \(\Sigma\in E_m\), all inclusions \(r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\) hold simultaneously.  Therefore
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\text{ for all }1\le j\le J
 \right)\ge1-\alpha.
\]
This covers every retained branch and selects none.

Assume \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)=\{r_1(\Sigma)\}\) throughout \(\mathcal K_G\).  On the events \(\mathcal H_m\) from \(\mathrm{thm:regular\mbox{-}finite\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}inference}\), the estimated set is bijectively matched to this singleton.  Hence it has exactly one element, denoted \(\widehat r_m\), and
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\{\widehat r_m\}\right)\longrightarrow1.
\tag{79}
\]
Define \(\widehat r_m=0\) off this event; (79) makes the modification uniformly negligible.  For singleton sets the Hausdorff distance is absolute error, so the rate conclusion of the preceding theorem gives
\[
 |\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)|=O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\]
uniformly, proving consistency.  Taking the sole coordinate of its joint branch limit yields
\[
 \sqrt m\{\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,W_{11}(\Sigma)),
\]
where
\[
 W(\Sigma)=Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The negligible modification does not affect the limit.  If \(W_{11}(\Sigma)=0\), the notation denotes the degenerate centered normal law; no variance lower bound is required.

Fix one source-consistent recorded stratum and invoke \(\mathrm{def:source\mbox{-}prime\mbox{-}chart}\).  Thus \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\), \(r\le2k\), \(P=\ker\xi\subset K_G[x]\), and chart validity gives
\[
 PK_G[x]_{H\Delta}
 =(h_1,\ldots,h_c)K_G[x]_{H\Delta},
 \qquad \xi(H\Delta)\ne0,
\tag{36}
\]
where \(c=\operatorname{ht}P\), the localized sequence is reduced and regular, and \(\Delta\) is a nonzero \(c\)-by-\(c\) Jacobian minor.  Therefore (36) presents the localization of the source prime rather than an extraneous residual component.  It is smooth and pure dimensional of dimension
\[
 q=r-c\le2k.
\tag{37}
\]
The principal open set is encoded polynomially by adjoining \(u\) and \(uH\Delta-1=0\).

Put \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  The hypothesis \(d_e(G)<\infty\) and characteristic zero make \(E/K_G\) finite separable.  For every \(K_G\)-embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the algebra \(L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}\) is nonzero: choose an \(E\)-transcendence basis of \(L\), after which the remaining extension is algebraic, and use faithful flatness of field extension.  Hence the base-changed source-prime chart has a nonempty component above every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\), with \(H\Delta\) nonzero on it.

Generic affine hyperplanes meet each positive-dimensional component properly.  There are only \(d_e(G)\) conjugate components, so the intersection of their nonempty open sets of admissible choices is nonempty.  Choose \(q\) affine linear forms whose successive intersections are transverse, zero dimensional, and nonempty on every conjugate component.  This is the transverse slicing operation covered by \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\); randomized choices outside the finitely many determinant and leading-form hypersurfaces have the required property.

Apply that lemma to the localized regular sequence and the \(q\) slices.  On successful choices it returns a finite reduced algebra \(B_{\mathfrak C}\), multiplication matrices, and a primitive-element representation.  The chart's rational lifting circuits recover every eliminated directed coordinate, including \(\lambda_e\), and their validity identities make every original residual vanish in the source-prime localization.  Let \(M_{e,\mathfrak C}\) denote multiplication by the recovered \(\lambda_e\), and put
\[
 \chi_{e,\mathfrak C}(t)=\det(tI-M_{e,\mathfrak C}).
\tag{38}
\]
Every root recorded by (38) is a conjugate of \(\lambda_e\).  Conversely, the common slices meet every conjugate component, so every conjugate occurs for at least one chart.  It follows that
\[
 p_e(t)=\operatorname{sqfree}\!\left(
   \prod_{\mathfrak C}\chi_{e,\mathfrak C}(t)
 \right),
 \qquad \deg p_e=d_e(G).
\tag{39}
\]
Indeed, the right side is the unique monic polynomial whose roots are exactly the distinct \(K_G\)-conjugates of \(\lambda_e\).  This proves a single-coordinate claim even when the unsliced fiber is positive dimensional.

All chart coefficients and lifting maps are rational arithmetic circuits in covariance entries.  Determinants, multiplication-matrix operations, differentiation, subresultant greatest-common-divisor computation, squarefree extraction, and monic normalization are arithmetic-circuit operations over \(K_G\), so (39) gives rational circuits for every coefficient of \(p_e\).  For each lifting identity, clearing covariance denominators records its denominators and the resulting original-incidence identity.  Homogenization before slicing records projective leading forms; univariate normalization records the specialized leading coefficient and squarefreeness resultant.  Covariance-localization factors are retained separately, and real sign data are checked after substitution into the original residuals.  These finitely many nonzero circuits form \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\), and their repetition-free cleared product is \(h_{G,e}\).  Equation (36) and \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) ensure that no directed-coordinate expression is inverted, so every pole or identically zero-over-zero stratum is represented by a supplied valid chart or retained by an original-incidence check.

For arbitrary recorded equations and inequations use \(\mathrm{lem:lifting\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}equidimensional\mbox{-}decomposition}\); for regular localized slices use \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  Their complexity bounds, (37), multiplication-matrix linear algebra, and exact sign determination on the returned univariate representations give a universal \(a>0\) such that total arithmetic work and output length are at most
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^a
 \operatorname{poly}(\log(1/\delta)),
\tag{40}
\]
where \(s=s(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\) and \(\mathfrak d=\mathfrak d(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\).  The latter parameter includes all successive intersections, localizations, slices, and lifting fibers, so (40) charges every created branch.

Every randomized decision is a nonvanishing test for an explicit chart, transversality, leading-form, lifting, or resultant polynomial.  If their degree bounds are \(d_1,\ldots,d_M\), sample independently from finite sets \(S_j\) with \(d_j/|S_j|\le\delta/M\).  The Schwartz--Zippel lemma and a union bound give
\[
 \Pr(\text{some symbolic genericity decision is wrong})
 \le\sum_{j=1}^M\frac{d_j}{|S_j|}\le\delta.
\tag{41}
\]
On the complementary event, (36)--(39) prove that the returned tuple is exactly \((d_e(G),p_e,\mathcal Q_{G,e},h_{G,e})\).

Finally, if \(s\le n^b\) and \(\mathfrak d\le n^{b(k+1)}\), then for \(n\ge2\), after enlarging a constant,
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^a
 \le n^{a(\max\{1,b\}+1+b)(k+1)}
 \le n^{C(k+1)}.
\tag{42}
\]
This proves the fixed-parameter specialization.  The construction starts from a supplied valid localized source-prime chart and does not claim to select that embedded prime or construct its source-nonzero Jacobian minor.

For a finite simple graph \(H=(W,E_H)\) and \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^W\), put
\[
 c_H(r)=\left[\prod_{v\in W}X_v^{r_v}\right]
 \prod_{\{u,v\}\in E_H}(X_u+X_v).
\tag{80}
\]
Choosing \(X_v\) from the factor for \(\{u,v\}\) is equivalent to orienting that edge toward \(v\).  Thus \(c_H(r)\) counts orientations with indegree vector \(r\), and
\[
 c_H(r)=0\quad\text{unless}\quad
 \sum_{v\in W}r_v=|E_H|,qquad
 0\le r_v\le\deg_H(v).
\tag{81}
\]

On at most two vertices, simplicity leaves at most one edge and its direction is fixed by \(r\), so the count is at most one.  On at most three vertices, a forest has at most one orientation with prescribed indegrees: the orientation of an edge at a leaf is forced by the leaf's required indegree, and induction deletes that leaf.  For a triangle, the two directed cycles both have score \((1,1,1)\), while every transitive orientation is uniquely determined by its labeled permutation of \((0,1,2)\).  Hence the maximum on three vertices is two.

Now suppose \(|W|\le4\).  With at most four edges, every connected component is a tree except possibly one unicyclic component.  Repeated leaf deletion forces all edges off the unique cycle, and at most the two cyclic orientations remain.  Therefore
\[
 c_H(r)\le2\qquad(|W|\le4,\ |E_H|\le4).
\tag{82}
\]
With five edges, \(H\) is \(K_4\) minus one edge, say \(\{1,2\}\).  Conditional on the required indegrees \(a\) and \(b\) of vertices \(1\) and \(2\), direct collection in
\[
 (X_1+X_3)(X_1+X_4)(X_2+X_3)(X_2+X_4)(X_3+X_4)
\]
gives the maximum coefficient over the remaining two exponents as
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
  &b=0&b=1&b=2\\ \hline
 a=0&1&2&1\\
 a=1&2&3&2\\
 a=2&1&2&1.
 \end{array}
\tag{83}
\]
To verify the table, choose the \(a\) edges into vertex \(1\) and the \(b\) edges into vertex \(2\) among their two incident edges; the final edge \(\{3,4\}\) adds one to exactly one remaining indegree.  Grouping the \(\binom2a\binom2b\) choices by the two remaining indegrees gives (83).  Thus every five-edge coefficient is at most three.

With six edges, \(H=K_4\).  Up to permutation, the score vectors allowed by (81) are
\[
 (0,0,3,3),\ (0,1,2,3),\ (0,2,2,2),\
 (1,1,1,3),\ (1,1,2,2).
\tag{84}
\]
